tldr: A sampling-based whole-body model predictive control (MPC) approach enables a humanoid robot to lean against a table for support, extending its reaching distance by about 50 cm beyond normal upright standing. The system was validated on real hardware running at 34 Hz on a laptop without external motion capture.
hero_caption: Three-stage sequence of leaning over a table to reach far-away objects on the real robot (top) and in the MuJoCo simulator (bottom). By resting its forearm on the table to widen its support base, the robot extends its reaching reach to 130 cm—about 50 cm beyond its normal upright reach of about 80 cm—and can sustain the posture stably for over 4 minutes.
overview:
When humans reach for an object deep across a table, we naturally lean forward, bracing a hand or elbow against the surface to support our weight. For humanoid robots, however, establishing contact with the environment using body parts other than the feet, bearing load, and then returning to a stand has been an exceptionally difficult challenge. Conventional whole-body control typically aims to avoid contact or relies on pre-planned contact sequences with trajectory optimization, almost always requiring high-precision external motion capture systems.

To tackle this, the authors developed an approach using sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) running directly within the mature MuJoCo physics engine, solved online in real time (approx. 34 Hz) on a laptop CPU. Its key strength is using gradient-free sampling methods—such as the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)—to handle the physical discontinuities caused by making and breaking contact. Furthermore, by fusing foot kinematic odometry and head-mounted AprilTag visual tracking via a Kalman filter, they created a self-contained system completely free of external motion capture.

Experiments on the real Unitree H1-2 humanoid demonstrated an extended reach of about 50 cm compared to standing upright, reaching targets up to roughly 1.3 m away. Across 54 trials varying table heights and target positions, the robot achieved an 89% reach success rate and an 81% full reach-and-recovery success rate, demonstrating remarkable robustness. This notable study shows that a straightforward formulation can achieve dynamic, contact-rich whole-body behaviors by actively using environmental contact to its advantage.
contributions: Demonstrated on real hardware an online whole-body MPC that explicitly leverages non-foot environmental contact (bracing a forearm on a table) to extend humanoid workspace by approximately 50 cm
Adopted sampling-based MPC robust to contact discontinuities, achieving real-time 34 Hz control on a standalone consumer laptop (AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370)
Enabled sustained posture holding for over 4 minutes without external motion capture, relying solely on onboard proprioceptive sensors (IMU, joint encoders) fused with AprilTag vision and kinematics
Showed adaptability across 54 hardware trials over varying table heights and reach targets, and thoroughly analyzed the parametric operating limits of sampling-based planners in simulation

sections.heading: Leaning on a Table Like a Human to Reach Farther
sections.summary: Supported reaching—bracing against surfaces such as tables—is essential for humanoids to interact with objects beyond arm's length. This section introduces how a straightforward sampling-based MPC solves this challenge online on hardware in real time without large-scale reinforcement learning or complex trajectory optimization.
sections.details:
Whole-body humanoid control has advanced rapidly thanks to large-scale reinforcement learning and dedicated trajectory optimization. However, many of these approaches demand massive task-specific training data or predefined motion trajectories, and they often rely on elaborate external motion capture setups to circumvent state estimation noise and drift.

In real-world applications such as electric vehicle battery dismantling, many components are completely unreachable without leaning over a workbench. Humans routinely plant a hand or forearm onto the table to shift their weight, effortlessly supporting the large moment arm of an inclined posture, and then return to an upright stance. This movement involves contact timing and friction uncertainties while pushing the body far outside the support polygon of the feet, presenting an exceptionally demanding benchmark for robot control.

The authors therefore extended modern physics-based model predictive control (MPC) concepts to multi-contact planning and control (MCPC). Without relying on expensive external tracking hardware, the goal is to execute the entire cycle of leaning, reaching far away, and recovering to a stand on a commercial Unitree H1-2 humanoid robot.

captions.F1: A sequence showing forearm-braced leaning and reaching on the real robot and in simulation. Bracing the forearm on the table allows the robot to reach and track targets situated roughly 50 cm beyond its unbraced standing workspace limit (approx. 80 cm).

sections.heading: Multi-Contact Planning and the Evolution of MuJoCo MPC
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work in whole-body control exploiting environmental contact (MCPC) alongside recent developments in MuJoCo MPC (MJPC). The proposed approach stands out as a real-time online controller that accepts target coordinates without pre-fixing contact sequences.
sections.details:
### Whole-Body Control and Multi-Contact (MCPC)
Whole-body control involving non-foot contact has a long history. A classic approach divides the problem into two stages: first planning the contact sequence (where and when to make contact), and then optimizing whole-body trajectories and contact forces under those constraints. Representative examples include SEIKO, which achieved supported reaching on the position-controlled TALOS humanoid, and Opt2Skill, which tracks contact-optimized Crocoddyl trajectories using reinforcement learning. However, these methods require an explicit pre-planned contact schedule or offline trajectory generation. In contrast, this work directly accepts the geometry and object goal positions to solve contact-rich reaching online in real time.

### MuJoCo MPC (MJPC) Developments
MJPC, an interactive predictive control tool backed by the MuJoCo physics engine, has demonstrated strong real-world transfer for quadruped locomotion and Unitree H1 manipulation and locomotion. Most previous efforts, however, employed gradient-based methods such as iLQR (Iterative Linear Quadratic Regulator) and usually relied on external motion capture. This paper extends the framework to the Unitree H1-2 (which adds two extra degrees of freedom), applies derivative-free sampling planners, and operates completely without external motion capture.

sections.heading: Realizing Supported Reaching with Sampling-Based MPC and State Estimation
sections.summary: This section explains the mathematics of sampling-based MPC designed for contact discontinuities and details the 39 cost residuals modeling the leaning task. It also covers the Kalman filter state estimator that fuses foot kinematics with AprilTag tracking to dramatically reduce position drift.
sections.details:
### III-A MPC Formulation and Sampling Methods
The controller implements receding-horizon control, rolling out predictions 1 second ahead ($T=1$ s) inside the MuJoCo simulator and sending the initial control action $u_0$ to the real robot. In contact-rich problems, physics becomes discontinuous at contact impacts and friction boundaries, causing finite-difference Jacobians to easily get trapped in poor local minima (failing to discover contact).

To circumvent this, the authors adopted derivative-free sampling-based planners. Control candidates ($N=20$) generated by perturbing a nominal spline trajectory are simulated in parallel within MuJoCo, and their cumulative costs are evaluated. The paper benchmarks Predictive Sampling (PS), which selects the single best candidate; MPPI, which computes an exponentially weighted average; and CEM (Cross-Entropy Method) / iCEM, which iteratively refines the sampling distribution from an elite set. CEM proved to be the most robust planner against disturbances and model mismatches and was chosen as the default.

### III-B Task Modes and Cost Design
Control progresses through three modes: (1) Stand, (2) Reach, and (3) Recover. The overall task is parameterized by 39 residual cost terms across nine groups, including balance terms that keep the capture point $c_{\rm cp}$ (a balance metric based on center-of-mass position and velocity) within the support polygon, target tracking terms, and a "Brace" term encouraging the forearm onto the table. When the support link (forearm) enters within 10 mm of the table, the support surface is considered extended to the table, and the balance metric area expands automatically.

### III-C State Estimation Without External Motion Capture
To estimate the robot's base position and velocity, the authors built a random-walk Kalman filter model fusing the IMU, joint encoders, and foot kinematic odometry. However, purely integrating kinematic odometry drifts over time. To eliminate this drift, an onboard camera (Intel RealSense D435i) tracks an AprilTag placed on the work surface, and the resulting visual pose measurements are periodically fused into the Kalman filter.

sections.heading: Hardware Validation on H1-2: Extending Reach by 50 cm and the Secrets of Stability
sections.summary: Comprehensive experiments were conducted both in simulation and on the real robot. Results demonstrate a 50 cm reach extension, an 89% reach success rate across different table heights and targets, the mechanical causes of failure, and why sampling planners succeed at a planning rate of only 34 Hz.
sections.details:
### IV-A State Estimation Benchmark
Estimators were evaluated during stationary standing trials. Proprioception alone (IMU + leg odometry) accumulated horizontal drift at $+267$ mm/min (drifting roughly 0.48 m in 2 minutes), while LiDAR odometry via FAST-LIO drifted at $+210$ mm/min. In contrast, the "Internal + Fiducial" setup incorporating AprilTag visual observations dropped drift to $+4$ mm/min, a roughly 60-fold reduction.

### IV-B Supported Reaching and Recovery Evaluation
Measuring reach from the ankle to the gripper tip, unbraced upright standing reached roughly 80 cm, whereas maximal forearm-braced reaching achieved $123\pm 4$ cm in simulation and $130\pm 10$ cm on hardware—extending reach by about 50 cm. Center-of-mass margins remained positive, and postures were held stably for over 4 minutes. High-frequency end-effector jitter ($>1$ Hz) stayed at an exceptionally quiet $1.5\pm 0.4$ mm RMS in both simulation and hardware during commanded reaches.

### IV-C Why Do Failures Occur? Mechanics of Success vs. Failure
Examining the maximal reaching trials (11 successes, 4 failures out of 15), the differentiator lay in how load was transferred to the forearm. In successful runs, normal load built up smoothly to an average of roughly 125 N, and the shoulder pitch torque stabilized around $+10$ Nm (maintaining a geometry where the shoulder remains behind the elbow). In failed runs, contact delivered a sudden impact of about 150 N, pitching the shoulder ahead of the elbow and flipping torque to $-20$ to $-25$ Nm, which caused the robot to buckle forward.

### IV-D Generalization Across Table Heights and Target Coordinates
Across three table heights (0.935 m, 0.985 m, and 1.035 m) and six target positions ($20\text{ cm}\times 10\text{ cm}$ grid), totaling 54 trials without retuning controller parameters, the robot achieved an 89% reaching success rate (48/54) and an 81% full recovery rate (44/54). The average 3D reaching error was tight at $2.7\pm 0.9$ cm.

### IV-E Cost and Planner Ablations
Why does control succeed with only 20 samples at a relatively modest 34 Hz planning frequency? Simulation ablations revealed that high-gain joint PD controllers stabilize the posture between MPC updates, while action temporal persistence (holding sampled actions for at least 0.22 s) is critical for contact dynamics to actually emerge. Furthermore, across model mismatches (mass, joint stiffness, and friction offsets), CEM exhibited the widest operational basin, significantly outperforming PS and MPPI.

Crosses indicate targets, dashed circles indicate the 4 cm tolerance radius, and dots represent measured positions. Reaching completed accurately for almost all targets, with misses (marked with an X) occurring only at the two farthest points on the highest table.

sections.heading: Challenges for Deployment and the Future of Whole-Body Contact Control
sections.summary: This section summarizes the achievements of extending workspace without external motion capture while noting that an 81% full-cycle success rate leaves room for improvement for full autonomy, highlighting future directions like GPU parallelization and tactile sensing.
sections.details:
This study showed that a commercial humanoid can drastically expand its workspace by leaning on a table, enabled by sim-to-real transfer of a straightforward sampling-based MPC. Executing contact-rich dynamic motions using only onboard sensing and a camera—without expensive external motion tracking infrastructure—marks a major step toward practical robotic deployment.

On the other hand, an 81% full-cycle success rate means reliability is not yet high enough for completely unattended operation. The authors outline several directions for future work: smarter automatic selection of contact locations, recovery while holding payloads of unknown mass, generalizing to slopes and varied contact surfaces, and integrating rich tactile feedback from artificial skin sensors. Furthermore, recent high-performance CPUs and GPUs could push planning rates beyond 60 Hz, which is expected to boost the reliability of contact-rich control even further as computing hardware advances.

takeaways: Even in tasks with severe contact discontinuities, gradient-free sampling MPC (especially CEM) is fully capable of whole-body control on real hardware at planning rates around 30 Hz.
When generating sampled control sequences, maintaining action temporal persistence of at least 0.2 s is critical for discovering and evaluating contact dynamics in physics simulation.
Without external motion capture, fusing kinematic odometry with low-frequency landmark observations (AprilTag) is sufficient to maintain stable contact postures for minutes.
Treating environmental contact as a valuable ally that extends the support base—rather than an obstacle to avoid—can dramatically increase a humanoid robot's reach by 50 cm or more.
limitations: The overall full-cycle success rate remains at 81%, with failure modes where excessive initial impact load on the bracing arm causes the robot to buckle forward.
The bracing link (forearm) and table contact surface are predefined, lacking the ability to autonomously discover and select arbitrary body links for support based on the environment.
To prevent slipping between the aluminum frame and the table, rubber tape was applied to artificially elevate friction (handling diverse real-world friction conditions remains an open challenge).
